protections: A store name may not leave the store root: resolveWritePath compares Abs(name) with workingDir through filepath.Rel and rejects a '../' result (content/file/file.go:609-628).
A tar member may not leave the layer directory: resolveRelToBase relates the member name to the layer dir and rejects a '../' relative result (content/file/utils.go:231-244).
No symbolic link may sit between the layer dir and a member path: each walked parent is Lstat'ed in resolveRelToBase and rejected when it is a symlink (content/file/utils.go:246-257).

A link target must resolve inside the layer dir: ensureLinkPath joins the target onto the link's directory and reuses the two containment checks above before os.Symlink/os.Link is called (content/file/utils.go:264-275).
A store name is pushed at most once, and with DisableOverwrite not onto an existing path (content/file/file.go:261-268, 629-635).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: ensureLinkPath already validates every link target against the layer dir, and a target whose lexical clean is the layer dir itself is indistinguishable from '.', so the target reads as contained and the check as complete.

the 'no symbolic link allowed between base and target' loop reads as a check on the whole destination, but it starts at filepath.Dir(path) and stops at '.', so the final component of a member is never inspected before the file is opened.

the inline comment states that ORAS does not generate hard links and calls the behaviour a known limitation that will not be addressed, so hard-link members look out of scope for a pull-hardening fix.

the report and the extraction guards are about tar members; resolveWritePath already rejects '..' names, and a plain file push (or the layer dir created by pushDir) is a different API that never had a symlink check.

the name status map is a duplicate-name and concurrency aid rather than a path check, and the path actually written is still confined by resolveWritePath, so two spellings of one path look like a naming nicety.

masking: T4's outside-root write through a store name only becomes reachable once a symlink pointing outside the root exists under the root; T1 is a route that brings one into being.
T2's unchecked final component only lands outside the root once a link target resolves outside the layer dir; T1 supplies that resolution.

conflicts.what: T4's natural fix resolves symlinks when turning a store name into a path (EvalSymlinks), returning a different spelling when the store root itself is reached through a symlink; T1's member containment compares against that base, so both fixes must agree on one base spelling or every legitimate in-layer symlink member starts failing.

closing the name-alias gap by normalising the layer title also changes the prefix that tar members are written with (tarDirectory uses the title as prefix, content/file/utils.go:57-62), so layers already published under a non-normalised title stop extracting.

fairness_risks: Relative symlink targets that climb and come back inside the layer dir are legitimate and unit-tested (content/file/utils_test.go:212-217; content/file/file_unix_test.go:31-131); a rule that rejects any '..' in a link target would refuse them.
Absolute symlink targets pointing inside the layer dir must keep extracting (content/file/file_unix_test.go:133-248); rejecting absolute targets outright is not an acceptable rule.
Re-extraction over an existing symlink must keep succeeding (content/file/file_unix_test.go:250-404), so 'never remove or overwrite an existing member' cannot be the security rule.
Hard-link members with absolute linknames must keep extracting (content/file/utils_test.go:336-363).
AllowPathTraversalOnWrite=true must still write outside the root (content/file/file_test.go:2150-2207), so any new traversal rule has to be conditional on the default mode.

The store root may legitimately be reached through a symlinked path; several tests EvalSymlinks their temp root before use (content/file/file_test.go:232, content/file/file_unix_test.go:136, content/file/file_unix_test.go:336), so a symlink-resolving fix must not reject such a root.

design.why: Four independent groups with four different dismissals. The extraction link validation (T1+T2) is the advisory route and is a how-type mechanism: the target is checked after filepath.Join cleans it while the OS resolves the literal stored target, and the final component is never inspected, so a solver who reads ensureLinkPath and the Lstat loop believes the lane is closed. T3 sits in the same helper but is dismissible on the code's own words ('known limitation and will not be addressed') and is applied through a path the guard never reconstructs. T4 is a parallel sink (plain push and the pushDir base) that never received the extraction symlink guard, dismissible because the report only speaks about extraction. T5 is a different object class (name identity vs resolved path) with a benign-sounding dismissal. Together they force a solver to touch link-target validation, final-component checking, hard-link handling and name-to-path resolution, which no single guard closes, while T1 and T3 in particular separate a deepseek-style miss (dismissed route) from a mimo-style miss (how-type mechanism).

unverified: The A and B fix diffs (cc323e564d90, adab2f25ea95) are outside this worktree; which guard A added and which hole B's fix closed is inferred from the code shape and from the issue references in tests (#402 content/file/file_unix_test.go:31, #865 content/file/file_unix_test.go:250), not read from the commits. The H3 assignment is therefore inferred.

That the hidden B test uses exactly the link-target shape described in T1 (a target whose lexical clean stays at the layer dir while the literal target is resolved component-wise by the kernel); the advisory text was only available as the candidate summary.

Add() makes an arbitrary caller-supplied path absolute with no root containment and maps digest to that path (content/file/file.go:420-428, 668-673), so Fetch can later reopen an outside file. It is not counted as a trap because the path is supplied by the local caller rather than by the pulled artifact.
Windows-specific path handling (drive-relative names, backslash separators) was not analysed; the package has no windows-specific source or test file, only !windows test builds.
